verdicts.summary: An established, official PC mod repository. The site itself is legitimate, but any downloaded mod file still needs basic caution.
verdicts.whatItIs: A long-running mod-hosting site for PC games, with an official domain and moderation. It is a primary source for mods rather than a random file host.
scamPatterns: Look-alike domains that copy the Nexus Mods name to serve malware
Links to 'Nexus Mods' downloads shared in Discord DMs that point elsewhere
protectionsRequired: Download only from the real nexusmods.com domain
Scan downloaded files before running them
Check a mod's comments and file size for anything unexpected
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a mod you installed turned out to be malicious, disconnect the affected device from the network, change passwords for any account you signed into afterward from a clean device, and run a reputable malware scan.

verdicts.summary: An established, official mod platform. The platform is legitimate, but a 2023 malware incident showed that even major mod platforms can be abused.
verdicts.whatItIs: A widely-used mod and addon platform owned by a major publisher, used for Minecraft, World of Warcraft, and other games.
scamPatterns: Fake 'CurseForge' sites or download buttons on unrelated pages
Mods distributed outside CurseForge that claim to be 'the same mod'
protectionsRequired: Download only from curseforge.com
Prefer mods with many downloads and recent, consistent updates
Be wary of mods that ask for login credentials or install extra software
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a mod was malicious, remove it, scan the device, and rotate passwords for accounts used on that device. The Fracturiser/BleedingPipe incident showed infection can spread to other mod files.

verdicts.assetName: Grey-market game key resellers (G2A and similar)
verdicts.summary: Real marketplaces that sell game keys, but keys can be sourced from fraud or regional pricing and may later be revoked.
verdicts.whatItIs: Third-party marketplaces where sellers resell game keys, often cheaper than official stores. The marketplace is a real business, but the supply chain is not always legitimate.
scamPatterns: Sellers demanding payment outside the platform
Keys that are revoked later because they were purchased with stolen cards
Fake 'key generator' or 'key reseller' sites that only collect payment
protectionsRequired: Prefer official stores and authorized resellers
If using a marketplace, buy from high-reputation sellers and use the platform's payment protection
Understand the key may be revoked or regional-locked
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a key is revoked or the purchase was fraudulent, dispute the charge through the marketplace or your payment provider, and avoid buying more keys from that seller.

verdicts.assetName: Third-party skin trading and marketplace sites
verdicts.summary: Legitimate sites exist, but the category is dense with phishing pages and API-key scams that drain inventories.
verdicts.whatItIs: Sites that let players trade or sell in-game cosmetics (CS2 skins and similar) outside the official game ecosystem. Some are legitimate businesses; many are fronts.
scamPatterns: Fake login pages that steal your Steam credentials
Requests for your Steam API key, used to hijack trades
Middleman scams and fake trade offers
protectionsRequired: Never share your Steam API key or login session
Verify you are on the real site, not a look-alike
Prefer official in-game marketplaces where available
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If your inventory was drained or your account compromised, revoke your Steam API key, deauthorize all other devices, change your password, and enable Steam Guard if not already on.

verdicts.summary: Legitimate VPNs can protect your network, but the category includes aggressive marketing, latency trade-offs, and occasional fake or malware-laden 'VPN' apps.
verdicts.whatItIs: VPN services marketed to gamers for privacy, region access, or DDoS protection. Quality and honesty vary widely.
scamPatterns: Free 'gaming VPN' apps that bundle malware or sell your traffic
Fake VPN sites that look like well-known brands
protectionsRequired: Use a well-known, independently audited VPN provider
Read the privacy policy — a VPN should not log your traffic
Test latency honestly; a VPN usually adds ping, not removes it
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a VPN app turned out to be malicious, uninstall it, scan the device, and change passwords for accounts used while it was installed.

verdicts.summary: Paying someone to play on your account violates most games' terms and means handing your login to a stranger.
verdicts.whatItIs: Services where a third party logs into your account to raise your rank or complete content for a fee. It breaks platform rules and gives a stranger full access to your account.
scamPatterns: Boosters who keep the account or drain its items and payment methods
Fake 'boosting' sites that only steal credentials
protectionsRequired: Never share your password, session, or 2FA codes with anyone
Understand that boosting can get your account banned
Remove any authorized devices or sessions afterward if you did use one
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a booster stole your account, follow the platform's recovery flow immediately, revoke all sessions, change your password from a clean device, and enable 2FA.

verdicts.summary: Cheat downloads are one of the most common ways players get infected with info-stealing malware.
verdicts.whatItIs: Downloads advertised as free cheats, aimbots, or trainers. They are frequently bundled with credential stealers, and using cheats also violates game terms and can get you banned.
scamPatterns: Installers that require you to disable antivirus
Cheats that ask for your account login 'to activate'
Discord or YouTube links to 'undetected' cheats
protectionsRequired: Do not download or run cheat tools
If you already did, assume the device is compromised and act accordingly
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If you ran a cheat tool, disconnect the device, run a malware scan, change passwords for every account used on that device from a clean device, and enable 2FA.

verdicts.assetName: "Free skin / Nitro / V-Bucks / Riot Points" generators
verdicts.summary: There is no such thing as a free-currency generator — these are phishing and credential-theft fronts.
verdicts.whatItIs: Sites, bots, or messages promising free in-game currency, skins, or subscriptions. They collect logins or install stealers and deliver nothing.
scamPatterns: A 'generator' that asks for your username and password
Urgency and limited-time framing to make you act fast
A request to complete 'verification' by logging in through a fake page
protectionsRequired: Only get currency, skins, and subscriptions through official stores and promotions
Never enter your login on a third-party 'generator' page
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If you entered your credentials on a generator, change your password immediately from a clean device, enable 2FA, and revoke all sessions.

verdicts.summary: Buying an account usually means buying one that was stolen or will be recovered by the original owner — and the sale violates platform rules.
verdicts.whatItIs: Marketplaces and sellers offering accounts with games, skins, or ranks already unlocked. Most are stolen, and sellers often reclaim them after payment.
scamPatterns: Sellers who take the account back after the sale using recovery
Accounts that get banned because they were stolen or breached
Payment outside a protected channel
protectionsRequired: Do not buy or sell accounts — it violates terms and funds theft
Build your own account with 2FA enabled from day one
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If you bought an account that was reclaimed or banned, you have little recourse — platform support will not help recover an account you did not originally own.

verdicts.assetName: "Free Steam / PSN / Xbox gift card" sites
verdicts.summary: Sites promising free gift cards are survey-and-credential-collection scams, not giveaways.
verdicts.whatItIs: Pages that claim to reward you with gift cards after completing surveys or 'verification'. They harvest data, sign you up for paid services, or steal logins, and the card never arrives.
scamPatterns: A gift card requiring a survey or 'human verification' first
A reward that requires your login or card details to claim
protectionsRequired: Treat unsolicited gift-card offers as scams by default
Never enter login or payment details to 'claim' a reward
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If you entered details, watch for unauthorized charges, change passwords on any accounts you exposed, and report the page.

verdicts.assetName: "Verify your account" Discord QR-code and login scams
verdicts.summary: Scanning a QR code to 'verify' in a Discord server can hand your entire session to an attacker.
verdicts.whatItIs: A scam where a server asks you to scan a QR code or log in to 'verify' you are human. The QR is a legitimate Discord login QR, so scanning it logs the attacker's device into your account.
scamPatterns: Servers that require a QR 'verification' to access channels
Messages from 'Discord staff' asking you to confirm your login
protectionsRequired: Never scan a Discord login QR from an untrusted server or DM
Discord will never ask for your password, token, or login QR
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If your account was taken, change your password from a clean device, enable 2FA, and use Discord's official support flow to recover access and revoke sessions.

verdicts.summary: Anyone offering to recover your account for a fee is a scammer — recovery is always done through the official platform, free of charge.
verdicts.whatItIs: Individuals or services claiming they can 'hack back' or recover a stolen account for a fee. They take your money and either do nothing or steal the account outright.
scamPatterns: A request for payment or your login 'to recover' the account
Impersonation of platform support on Discord, Twitter, or email
protectionsRequired: Never pay a third party to recover an account
Recovery is always done through the platform's official support, free
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: Use the official recovery flow for your platform. Do not engage, pay, or share credentials with anyone offering recovery for a fee.

verdicts.summary: Pirated game downloads are a leading vector for malware bundled into the installer.
verdicts.whatItIs: Downloaded copies of games that bypass payment. The installers and 'cracks' are routinely used to bundle stealers, and the source cannot be trusted.
scamPatterns: Installers that demand antivirus be disabled
Torrents or links from unknown sites rather than official stores
protectionsRequired: Buy games from official stores and authorized resellers
Never run a 'crack' that requires disabling security software
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a pirated download was malicious, disconnect the device, scan it, and rotate passwords for all accounts used on it from a clean device.

verdicts.summary: Modded APK files from outside official app stores are a common way to install mobile malware.
verdicts.whatItIs: Modified Android app files offering 'unlimited coins' or 'premium unlocked' versions of games. They are not signed by the developer and are frequently repackaged with malware.
scamPatterns: APK downloads that request excessive permissions
'Mod' versions of games that ask for SMS, contacts, or overlay access
protectionsRequired: Install apps only from official app stores
Keep 'install from unknown sources' disabled
Be especially cautious where mobile money (e.g. M-Pesa) is linked to the device
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a mod APK was malicious, uninstall it, scan the device, revoke its permissions, and change passwords for accounts used on the device — especially any linked to payments.

verdicts.summary: Private servers and custom launchers are common and mostly fine, but they bypass official moderation and some bundle malware.
verdicts.whatItIs: Community-run Minecraft servers and launchers that are not operated by the game's developer. Many are legitimate communities; a minority distribute modified clients that steal credentials.
scamPatterns: Launchers that require your Microsoft/Minecraft login
Modified clients that ask for extra permissions or 'verify' with your account
protectionsRequired: Use well-known servers and launchers with an active community
Never enter your main account login in a third-party launcher
Keep your Microsoft account 2FA enabled
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: If a launcher or mod was malicious, remove it, scan the device, and rotate your Microsoft/Minecraft account password from a clean device.

verdicts.assetName: Fake Steam login pages and trade offers
verdicts.summary: Phishing pages that imitate Steam's login to steal your credentials and Steam Guard codes.
verdicts.whatItIs: Pages that copy Steam's design and ask you to log in — often reached through a 'trade offer' or 'item giveaway' link. They capture your password and sometimes your Steam Guard code in real time.
scamPatterns: A 'trade offer' or 'gift' link that opens a Steam-looking login
A login page that asks for your Steam Guard code more than once
protectionsRequired: Only log in on steampowered.com or steamcommunity.com
Check the address bar before entering credentials
Never enter your Steam Guard code on a page reached via a chat link
verdicts.whatToDoIfCompromised: Change your password immediately from a clean device, enable Steam Guard, deauthorize all other devices, and revoke your Steam API key if one was set.
